claim: Obesity is generally associated with insulin resistance in liver and muscle and increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes.
source: Obesity is generally associated with insulin resistance in liver and muscle and increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes, however there is a population of obese people that remain insulin sensitive.
evidence: This is a general statement about the relationship between obesity and insulin resistance, supported by established scientific consensus.

claim: There is a population of obese people that remain insulin sensitive.
source: Obesity is generally associated with insulin resistance in liver and muscle and increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes, however there is a population of obese people that remain insulin sensitive.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to existing literature about metabolically healthy obese individuals.

claim: Recent work suggests that mice fed high carbohydrate diets can become obese without apparent glucose intolerance.
source: Similarly, recent work suggests that mice fed high carbohydrate diets can become obese without apparent glucose intolerance.
evidence: This claim references recent research findings, implying citation-based support.

claim: Both Hi-ST and Hi-F mice accumulated a similar amount of fat and tissue triglyceride compared to chow-fed mice.
source: Both Hi-ST and Hi-F mice accumulated a similar amount of fat and tissue triglyceride compared to chow-fed mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of fat mass and tissue triglyceride levels presented in the manuscript.

claim: Hi-F diet mice developed glucose intolerance as well as liver and muscle insulin resistance.
source: However, while Hi-F diet mice developed glucose intolerance as well as liver and muscle insulin resistance (assessed via euglycaemic/hyperinsulinaemic clamp), obese Hi-ST mice maintained glucose tolerance and insulin action similar to lean, chow-fed controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by glucose tolerance tests and euglycaemic/hyperinsulinaemic clamp data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Obese Hi-ST mice maintained glucose tolerance and insulin action similar to lean, chow-fed controls.
source: However, while Hi-F diet mice developed glucose intolerance as well as liver and muscle insulin resistance (assessed via euglycaemic/hyperinsulinaemic clamp), obese Hi-ST mice maintained glucose tolerance and insulin action similar to lean, chow-fed controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by glucose tolerance tests and euglycaemic/hyperinsulinaemic clamp measurements.

claim: The preservation of insulin action despite obesity in Hi-ST mice was associated with differences in de novo lipogenesis.
source: This preservation of insulin action despite obesity in Hi-ST mice was associated with differences in de novo lipogenesis and levels of C22:0 ceramide in liver and C18:0 ceramide in muscle.
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements of de novo lipogenesis rates presented in the manuscript.

claim: The preservation of insulin action despite obesity in Hi-ST mice was associated with levels of C22:0 ceramide in liver.
source: This preservation of insulin action despite obesity in Hi-ST mice was associated with differences in de novo lipogenesis and levels of C22:0 ceramide in liver and C18:0 ceramide in muscle.
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomic analysis data showing ceramide levels in liver.

claim: The preservation of insulin action despite obesity in Hi-ST mice was associated with levels of C18:0 ceramide in muscle.
source: This preservation of insulin action despite obesity in Hi-ST mice was associated with differences in de novo lipogenesis and levels of C22:0 ceramide in liver and C18:0 ceramide in muscle.
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomic analysis data showing ceramide levels in muscle.

claim: Dietary manipulation can influence insulin action independently of the level of adiposity.
source: This indicates that dietary manipulation can influence insulin action independently of the level of adiposity and that the presence of specific ceramide species correlates with these differences.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing different insulin sensitivity outcomes despite similar adiposity levels.

claim: The presence of specific ceramide species correlates with differences in insulin action.
source: This indicates that dietary manipulation can influence insulin action independently of the level of adiposity and that the presence of specific ceramide species correlates with these differences.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis between ceramide levels and insulin sensitivity measures.

claim: The degree of insulin resistance does not always correlate with the extent of obesity.
source: However, the degree of insulin resistance does not always correlate with the extent of obesity (Gan et al., 2003) and there exists a population of individuals who are obese yet exhibit no difference in insulin action compared to groups of lean individuals (Tonks et al., 2016), and lean individuals who are metabolically unhealthy (Stefan et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: There exists a population of individuals who are obese yet exhibit no difference in insulin action compared to groups of lean individuals.
source: However, the degree of insulin resistance does not always correlate with the extent of obesity (Gan et al., 2003) and there exists a population of individuals who are obese yet exhibit no difference in insulin action compared to groups of lean individuals (Tonks et al., 2016), and lean individuals who are metabolically unhealthy (Stefan et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tonks et al., 2016.

claim: There are lean individuals who are metabolically unhealthy.
source: However, the degree of insulin resistance does not always correlate with the extent of obesity (Gan et al., 2003) and there exists a population of individuals who are obese yet exhibit no difference in insulin action compared to groups of lean individuals (Tonks et al., 2016), and lean individuals who are metabolically unhealthy (Stefan et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Stefan et al., 2017.

claim: The mechanisms behind the different metabolic profiles in equally obese individuals remain unclear.
source: These reports of obese individuals with preserved insulin action have led to the recognition of a population described as metabolically healthy obese (MHO) but the mechanisms behind the different metabolic profiles in equally obese individuals remain unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific knowledge regarding MHO mechanisms.

claim: It has been suggested that MHO individuals are simply on a different trajectory to more overt metabolic dysfunction.
source: It has been suggested that MHO individuals are simply on a different trajectory to more overt metabolic dysfunction but there is also the possibility that genetic background, body fat distribution, or diet and exercise history might influence the relationship between obesity and insulin action (Vilela et al., 2021; Gómez-Zorita et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim references suggestions from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: Genetic background, body fat distribution, or diet and exercise history might influence the relationship between obesity and insulin action.
source: It has been suggested that MHO individuals are simply on a different trajectory to more overt metabolic dysfunction but there is also the possibility that genetic background, body fat distribution, or diet and exercise history might influence the relationship between obesity and insulin action (Vilela et al., 2021; Gómez-Zorita et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Vilela et al., 2021 and Gómez-Zorita et al., 2021.

claim: Animal models used to investigate the mechanistic relationship between obesity and metabolic dysfunction normally employ a Hi-F diet regime (45–60% of total calories) to produce obesity and insulin resistance.
source: Animal models used to investigate the mechanistic relationship between obesity and metabolic dysfunction normally employ a Hi-F diet regime (45–60% of total calories) to produce obesity and insulin resistance (reviewed in Small et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a review citation to Small et al., 2018.

claim: The level of insulin resistance observed in animal models does not necessarily correlate with the accumulation of fat in diet-induced obesity.
source: As with humans, the level of insulin resistance observed in animal models does not necessarily correlate with the accumulation of fat in diet-induced obesity.
evidence: This is a general observation about animal models, supported by established knowledge.

claim: Insulin action measured by hyperinsulinaemic/euglycaemic clamp or glucose tolerance tests is decreased after 2 or 3 weeks of feeding a Hi-F diet but does not significantly worsen over the subsequent 10–20 weeks even though the animals continue to accumulate fat and become obese.
source: It has been observed in mice and rats that insulin action measured by hyperinsulinaemic/euglycaemic clamp or glucose tolerance tests is decreased after 2 or 3 weeks of feeding a Hi-F diet but does not significantly worsen over the subsequent 10–20 weeks even though the animals continue to accumulate fat and become obese (Turner et al., 2013; Turner et al., 2007; Burchfield et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Turner et al., 2013; Turner et al., 2007; Burchfield et al., 2018.

claim: Some strains of mice can become obese eating a Hi-F diet without deleterious effects on glucose tolerance.
source: There are also data showing that some strains of mice can become obese eating a Hi-F diet without deleterious effects on glucose tolerance (Montgomery et al., 2013a; Stöckli et al., 2017; Appiakannan et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Montgomery et al., 2013a; Stöckli et al., 2017; Appiakannan et al., 2020.

claim: Genetic makeup can impact the relationship between obesity and glucoregulation.
source: Clearly genetic makeup can impact the relationship between obesity and glucoregulation, but less is known about the relative importance of diet composition and total fat mass in the regulation of insulin action at the whole body and tissue level.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies showing strain differences in mice.

claim: Less is known about the relative importance of diet composition and total fat mass in the regulation of insulin action at the whole body and tissue level.
source: Clearly genetic makeup can impact the relationship between obesity and glucoregulation, but less is known about the relative importance of diet composition and total fat mass in the regulation of insulin action at the whole body and tissue level.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific knowledge.

claim: Mice fed diets lower in protein and fat and higher in carbohydrate had the greatest median lifespan.
source: In a study assessing the impact of diet composition on longevity and metabolic health in mice, animals fed diets lower in protein and fat and higher in carbohydrate had the greatest median lifespan (Solon-Biet et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Solon-Biet et al., 2014.

claim: Mice on lower protein, higher carbohydrate diets exhibited better measures of glucose tolerance despite accumulating similar amounts of adipose tissue to mice on Hi-F diets that exhibited poor glucose tolerance.
source: Interestingly, mice on these lower protein, higher carbohydrate diets also exhibited better measures of glucose tolerance despite accumulating similar amounts of adipose tissue to mice on Hi-F diets that exhibited poor glucose tolerance (Solon-Biet et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Solon-Biet et al., 2014.

claim: Mice fed a Hi-ST diet had a similar body weight trajectory to that of mice fed a Hi-F diet.
source: Mice fed a Hi-ST diet had a similar body weight trajectory to that of mice fed a Hi-F diet and by the end of the feeding period, both these groups were heavier than the chow controls and there was no significant difference in body weight between Hi-ST and Hi-F fed mice (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 1A.

claim: By the end of the feeding period, both Hi-ST and Hi-F groups were heavier than the chow controls.
source: Mice fed a Hi-ST diet had a similar body weight trajectory to that of mice fed a Hi-F diet and by the end of the feeding period, both these groups were heavier than the chow controls and there was no significant difference in body weight between Hi-ST and Hi-F fed mice (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: There was no significant difference in body weight between Hi-ST and Hi-F fed mice.
source: Mice fed a Hi-ST diet had a similar body weight trajectory to that of mice fed a Hi-F diet and by the end of the feeding period, both these groups were heavier than the chow controls and there was no significant difference in body weight between Hi-ST and Hi-F fed mice (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of body weight data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The increase in body weight was due to an increase in fat mass as lean mass was similar between the three groups.
source: Body composition measured at 4, 6, and 12 weeks showed that this increase in body weight was due to an increase in fat mass as lean mass was similar between the three groups (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by body composition measurements shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Mice on the two dietary interventions consumed more energy per day compared to the control chow-fed group.
source: Mice on the two dietary interventions consumed more energy per day compared to the control chow-fed group (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by food intake measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Energy expenditure (EE) was similar between groups.
source: Energy expenditure (EE) was similar between groups (Figure 1E and F) with mice displaying a positive relationship between body mass and EE regardless of diet (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by energy expenditure measurements shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Mice displayed a positive relationship between body mass and EE regardless of diet.
source: Energy expenditure (EE) was similar between groups (Figure 1E and F) with mice displaying a positive relationship between body mass and EE regardless of diet (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Ambulatory activity was not different between groups.
source: Ambulatory activity was not different between groups (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by activity measurements shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Hi-F fed mice displayed a lower respiratory quotient, indicating a higher ratio of lipid to carbohydrate oxidation.
source: Hi-F fed mice displayed a lower respiratory quotient (Figure 1I and J), indicating a higher ratio of lipid to carbohydrate oxidation, while Hi-ST mice showed an intermediate respiratory quotient between Hi-F mice and chow control mice possibly due to a higher dietary fat content of the Hi-ST diet compared to chow (calorically 21% vs. 6%, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by respiratory quotient measurements shown in Figure 1I and J, with interpretation based on established metabolic knowledge.

claim: Hi-ST mice showed an intermediate respiratory quotient between Hi-F mice and chow control mice possibly due to a higher dietary fat content of the Hi-ST diet compared to chow (calorically 21% vs. 6%, respectively).
source: Hi-F fed mice displayed a lower respiratory quotient (Figure 1I and J), indicating a higher ratio of lipid to carbohydrate oxidation, while Hi-ST mice showed an intermediate respiratory quotient between Hi-F mice and chow control mice possibly due to a higher dietary fat content of the Hi-ST diet compared to chow (calorically 21% vs. 6%, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by respiratory quotient data and diet composition information, with speculative reasoning about the cause.

claim: The Hi-F diet caused a decrease in glucose tolerance at both 4 and 12 weeks.
source: While the Hi-F diet caused the expected decrease in glucose tolerance at both time points, glucose tolerance in the Hi-ST mice, remained very similar to chow control mice, even though Hi-ST mice had similar levels of adiposity as the Hi-F mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by oral glucose tolerance test data shown in Figure 2A-F.

claim: Glucose tolerance in the Hi-ST mice remained very similar to chow control mice, even though Hi-ST mice had similar levels of adiposity as the Hi-F mice.
source: While the Hi-F diet caused the expected decrease in glucose tolerance at both time points, glucose tolerance in the Hi-ST mice, remained very similar to chow control mice, even though Hi-ST mice had similar levels of adiposity as the Hi-F mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by glucose tolerance test data and body composition measurements.

claim: After both 4 and 12 weeks of diet, Hi-ST and Hi-F mice displayed a higher fasting and glucose-stimulated blood insulin concentration during the GTT compared to chow controls.
source: After both 4 and 12 weeks of diet, Hi-ST and Hi-F mice displayed a higher fasting and glucose-stimulated blood insulin concentration during the GTT compared to chow controls with Hi-ST mice returning to basal levels faster than the Hi-F group (Figure 2C and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by insulin measurements during GTT shown in Figure 2C and F.

claim: Hi-ST mice returned to basal insulin levels faster than the Hi-F group during the GTT.
source: After both 4 and 12 weeks of diet, Hi-ST and Hi-F mice displayed a higher fasting and glucose-stimulated blood insulin concentration during the GTT compared to chow controls with Hi-ST mice returning to basal levels faster than the Hi-F group (Figure 2C and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by insulin kinetics data shown in Figure 2C and F.

claim: Hi-ST mice had improved whole body glucose disposal during the oGTT when compared to Hi-F.
source: While the plasma 6,6-2H-glucose enrichment curves were similar in all three groups (Figure 2H), there was a significant and consistent difference in the exogenous glucose concentration curves, with Hi-F being higher than chow and Hi-ST (Figure 2I), thus indicating that Hi-ST mice had improved whole body glucose disposal during the oGTT when compared to Hi-F.
evidence: This claim is supported by stable isotope-labeled glucose data shown in Figure 2H and I.

claim: Hi-ST mice may have had a brief period of enhanced endogenous glucose production (EGP) suppression during the early period (0–30 min) of the OGTT compared to Hi-F mice.
source: When endogenous glucose levels were expressed as a change from baseline, there were only small changes evident between Hi-ST and Hi-F at 15 and 30 min post glucose load, suggesting that Hi-ST mice may have also had a brief period of enhanced endogenous glucose production (EGP) suppression during the early period (0–30 min) of the OGTT compared to Hi-F mice.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the endogenous glucose data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: The amount of insulin released from isolated islets in response to 16.7 mM glucose was similar in all groups.
source: The amount of insulin released from isolated islets in response to 16.7 mM glucose was similar in all groups (Figure 2K), however there was an increase in insulin content that was only significant in the Hi-F group (Figure 2L).
evidence: This claim is supported by glucose-stimulated insulin secretion measurements shown in Figure 2K.

claim: There was an increase in insulin content that was only significant in the Hi-F group.
source: The amount of insulin released from isolated islets in response to 16.7 mM glucose was similar in all groups (Figure 2K), however there was an increase in insulin content that was only significant in the Hi-F group (Figure 2L).
evidence: This claim is supported by insulin content measurements shown in Figure 2L.

claim: Inherent differences in islet function are not the driver of glucose tolerance differences observed in the Hi-ST fed and Hi-F fed mice.
source: Thus, it would appear that inherent differences in islet function are not the driver of glucose tolerance differences observed in the Hi-ST fed and Hi-F fed mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the islet function data showing similar insulin secretion responses.

claim: Blood glucose was maintained at euglycaemia (~8 mM) throughout the clamp.
source: Blood glucose was maintained at euglycaemia (~8 mM) throughout the clamp (Figure 3A) and plasma insulin levels were elevated to a similar extent by the insulin infusion between groups (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by blood glucose measurements during the clamp shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Plasma insulin levels were elevated to a similar extent by the insulin infusion between groups.
source: Blood glucose was maintained at euglycaemia (~8 mM) throughout the clamp (Figure 3A) and plasma insulin levels were elevated to a similar extent by the insulin infusion between groups (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by plasma insulin measurements during the clamp shown in Figure 3B.

claim: All three groups had similar basal NEFA and were able to suppress NEFA levels to a similar extent.
source: All three groups had similar basal NEFA (chow 0.73±0.07; Hi-ST 0.78±0.08; Hi-F 0.67±0.09 mM) and were able to suppress NEFA levels to a similar extent (chow 0.18±0.03; Hi-ST 0.22±0.03; Hi-F 0.29±0.05 mM).
evidence: This claim is supported by NEFA measurements during the clamp.

claim: The glucose infusion rate (GIR) needed to maintain euglycaemia was lower in the Hi-F animals compared to both the chow and Hi-ST, indicating a reduced whole body insulin action.
source: The glucose infusion rate (GIR) needed to maintain euglycaemia was lower in the Hi-F animals compared to both the chow and Hi-ST, indicating a reduced whole body insulin action (Figure 3C and D; p>0.05), while there was no significant difference in GIR between the obese Hi-ST and lean chow control mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by GIR measurements shown in Figure 3C and D, with interpretation based on established metabolic knowledge.

claim: There was no significant difference in GIR between the obese Hi-ST and lean chow control mice.
source: The glucose infusion rate (GIR) needed to maintain euglycaemia was lower in the Hi-F animals compared to both the chow and Hi-ST, indicating a reduced whole body insulin action (Figure 3C and D; p>0.05), while there was no significant difference in GIR between the obese Hi-ST and lean chow control mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of GIR data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The ability of insulin to suppress hepatic glucose output (HGO) was impaired in the Hi-F animals when compared to both the chow and Hi-ST groups.
source: Although there was no difference in the basal hepatic glucose production, the ability of insulin to suppress hepatic glucose output (HGO) was impaired in the Hi-F animals when compared to both the chow and Hi-ST groups (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by HGO measurements shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: There was preservation of skeletal and heart muscle insulin action in the Hi-ST mice, while the Hi-F showed reduced insulin action indicative of insulin resistance.
source: Tissue glucose uptake data clearly demonstrated that there was preservation of skeletal and heart muscle insulin action in the Hi-ST mice, while the Hi-F showed reduced insulin action indicative of insulin resistance (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by tissue glucose uptake measurements shown in Figure 3H.

claim: White adipose tissue (WAT) was insulin resistant in both the Hi-ST and Hi-F groups compared to controls.
source: White adipose tissue (WAT) however was insulin resistant in both the Hi-ST and Hi-F groups compared to controls (Figure 3I).
evidence: This claim is supported by WAT glucose uptake measurements shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Brown adipose tissue (BAT) glucose uptake was fully preserved in the Hi-ST group while being significantly reduced in the Hi-F fed animals.
source: On the other hand, brown adipose tissue (BAT) glucose uptake was fully preserved in the Hi-ST group while being significantly reduced in the Hi-F fed animals (Figure 3I).
evidence: This claim is supported by BAT glucose uptake measurements shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The differences in insulin sensitivity of liver or quadriceps muscle were not associated with significant differences in the phosphorylation status of Akt.
source: The differences in insulin sensitivity of liver or quadriceps muscle were not associated with significant differences in the phosphorylation status of Akt (Figure 3J and K, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by Akt phosphorylation measurements shown in Figure 3J and K.

claim: There were no differences in the phosphorylation status of Akt in either the epididymal or subcutaneous WAT.
source: There were also no differences in the phosphorylation status of Akt in either the epididymal or subcutaneous WAT (Figure 3L and M, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by Akt phosphorylation measurements in WAT shown in Figure 3L and M.

claim: Citrate synthase (CS) in liver showed an increase in the Hi-ST group.
source: Mitochondrial enzyme activities in the liver showed an increase in citrate synthase (CS) in the Hi-ST group while β-hydroxyacyl CoA dehydrogenase (βHAD) was increased in the Hi-F animals (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by enzyme activity measurements shown in Table 1.

claim: β-hydroxyacyl CoA dehydrogenase (βHAD) in liver was increased in the Hi-F animals.
source: Mitochondrial enzyme activities in the liver showed an increase in citrate synthase (CS) in the Hi-ST group while β-hydroxyacyl CoA dehydrogenase (βHAD) was increased in the Hi-F animals (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by enzyme activity measurements shown in Table 1.

claim: In muscle there were increases in CS and βHAD in both the Hi-ST and Hi-F groups.
source: In muscle there were increases in CS and βHAD in both the Hi-ST and Hi-F groups (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by enzyme activity measurements shown in Table 1.

claim: The Hi-F animals had a decrease in the activity of pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) in muscle.
source: The Hi-F animals also had a decrease in the activity of pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) in muscle but a lower activity of PDH in liver of Hi-F mice did not reach statistical significance.
evidence: This claim is supported by enzyme activity measurements shown in Table 1.

claim: A lower activity of PDH in liver of Hi-F mice did not reach statistical significance.
source: The Hi-F animals also had a decrease in the activity of pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) in muscle but a lower activity of PDH in liver of Hi-F mice did not reach statistical significance.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of enzyme activity data shown in Table 1.

claim: Metabolomic analysis of glycolytic and TCA cycle intermediates after insulin stimulation during the clamp showed very little change across the three dietary groups in both muscle and liver.
source: Metabolomic analysis of glycolytic and TCA cycle intermediates after insulin stimulation during the clamp showed very little change across the three dietary groups in both muscle (Supplementary file 1a) and liver (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolomic data presented in Supplementary files 1a and 1b.

claim: Preservation of insulin action at the whole body level in animals fed a Hi-ST diet is paralleled by a maintenance of insulin action at the tissue level (liver, skeletal muscle, BAT).
source: Taken together, this data shows that preservation of insulin action at the whole body level in animals fed a Hi-ST diet is paralleled by a maintenance of insulin action at the tissue level (liver, skeletal muscle, BAT) and this was associated with altered activity of enzymes responsible for the direct oxidation of glucose and fatty acids in muscle and liver, rather than alterations in Akt phosphorylation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined clamp and tissue-specific glucose uptake data.

claim: Preservation of insulin action in Hi-ST mice was associated with altered activity of enzymes responsible for the direct oxidation of glucose and fatty acids in muscle and liver, rather than alterations in Akt phosphorylation.
source: Taken together, this data shows that preservation of insulin action at the whole body level in animals fed a Hi-ST diet is paralleled by a maintenance of insulin action at the tissue level (liver, skeletal muscle, BAT) and this was associated with altered activity of enzymes responsible for the direct oxidation of glucose and fatty acids in muscle and liver, rather than alterations in Akt phosphorylation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from enzyme activity and Akt phosphorylation data.

claim: In diet-induced obese mice, hepatic insulin resistance seems to be the largest contributing factor to the lower GIR during a clamp.
source: Additionally, this data suggests that in diet-induced obese mice, hepatic insulin resistance seems to be the largest contributing factor to the lower GIR during a clamp, while during a GTT, hepatic and peripheral insulin resistance seems to make similar contributions to the relative glucose intolerance observed in Hi-F mice (Figure 2I and J).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the clamp and GTT data.

claim: During a GTT, hepatic and peripheral insulin resistance seems to make similar contributions to the relative glucose intolerance observed in Hi-F mice.
source: Additionally, this data suggests that in diet-induced obese mice, hepatic insulin resistance seems to be the largest contributing factor to the lower GIR during a clamp, while during a GTT, hepatic and peripheral insulin resistance seems to make similar contributions to the relative glucose intolerance observed in Hi-F mice (Figure 2I and J).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the GTT data shown in Figure 2I and J.

claim: The weights of three WAT depots (epididymal, subcutaneous, and retroperitoneal) increased in the Hi-ST and Hi-F groups.
source: Consistent with the increase in whole body fat mass in the Hi-ST and Hi-F groups, as determined by EchoMRI (Figure 1C), we saw an increase in the weights of three WAT depots (Figure 4A; epididymal [Epi], subcutaneous [SC], and retroperitoneal [RP]).
evidence: This claim is supported by tissue weight measurements shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Liver and BAT mass did not change with diet treatment.
source: Liver (control 1.1±0.3; Hi-ST 1.2±0.1; Hi-F 1.2±0.1 g) and BAT (Figure 4A) mass did not change with diet treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by tissue weight measurements.

claim: Adipocyte size in both the epididymal and subcutaneous fat pads were, on average, increased in animals fed Hi-ST and Hi-F when compared to chow.
source: Adipocyte size in both the epididymal and subcutaneous fat pads were, on average, increased in animals fed Hi-ST and Hi-F when compared to chow (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by adipocyte size measurements shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Plasma leptin levels increased in the Hi-ST and Hi-F animals.
source: As expected with the increase in fat mass, plasma leptin levels increased in the Hi-ST and Hi-F animals (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by plasma leptin measurements shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Plasma adiponectin levels were not different between the groups.
source: Plasma adiponectin levels were not different between the groups (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by plasma adiponectin measurements shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Total triglyceride levels in both muscle and liver showed a similar increase in the Hi-F and Hi-ST animals.
source: Interestingly, total triglyceride levels in both muscle and liver showed a similar increase in the Hi-F and Hi-ST animals (Figure 4F and G), despite the differences in glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by triglyceride measurements shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: Four weeks of feeding was sufficient to increase total triglyceride levels in the liver of Hi-F and Hi-ST animals compared to control.
source: Four weeks of feeding was sufficient to increase total triglyceride levels in the liver of Hi-F and Hi-ST animals compared to control (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by liver triglyceride measurements shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The increase in liver triglyceride was associated with a suppression of liver DNL in the Hi-F animals compared to controls, with an increase in DNL seen in the Hi-ST animals.
source: This increase in liver triglyceride was associated with a suppression of liver DNL in the Hi-F animals compared to controls, with an increase in DNL seen in the Hi-ST animals (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by DNL measurements shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There was no difference between the groups in the rates of DNL in BAT or WAT.
source: There was no difference between the groups in the rates of DNL in BAT or WAT (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by DNL measurements in BAT and WAT shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: The abundance of key lipogenic enzymes acetyl CoA carboxylase (ACC), fatty acid synthase (FAS), and stearoyl-CoA desaturase-1 (SCD-1) were increased in the Hi-ST animals and decreased in the Hi-F groups compared to chow controls.
source: This same pattern was also seen in the abundance of key lipogenic enzymes acetyl CoA carboxylase (ACC), fatty acid synthase (FAS), and stearoyl-CoA desaturase-1 (SCD-1), which were increased in the Hi-ST animals and decreased in the Hi-F groups compared to chow controls (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: Activities of ATP citrate lysase (ACL) and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PDH) mirrored the pattern of lipogenic enzyme abundance.
source: Activities of two other enzymes, ATP citrate lysase (ACL), involved in the production of cytosolic acetyl-CoA and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PDH), which generates NADPH that is used as a cofactor for lipogenesis, also mirrored these results (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by enzyme activity measurements shown in Figure 5G and H.

claim: Liver is the primary site of DNL in the mouse since the rate of DNL in this organ was much higher than in any of the WAT depots.
source: This data indicates that liver is the primary site of DNL in the mouse since the rate of DNL in this organ was much higher than in any of the WAT depots.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing DNL rates across different tissues.

claim: DNL is lower in the Hi-F animals that have abundant access to fat from the diet, and higher in the Hi-ST animals where fat accumulation depends largely on DNL conversion of dietary carbohydrate to fat.
source: The data also indicated that DNL is lower in the Hi-F animals that have abundant access to fat from the diet, and higher in the Hi-ST animals where fat accumulation depends largely on DNL conversion of dietary carbohydrate to fat.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from DNL measurements and diet composition.

claim: In both the liver and the muscle, lipidomic analysis confirmed an increase in total triglyceride content that was similar in both Hi-ST and Hi-F groups.
source: In both the liver and the muscle, this lipidomic analysis confirmed an increase in total triglyceride content that was similar in both Hi-ST and Hi-F groups (Figure 6A and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomic data shown in Figure 6A and E.

claim: Total DAG levels were similarly increased in both dietary groups, in both tissues.
source: Total DAG levels were similarly increased in both dietary groups, in both tissues (Figure 6A and E), and not surprisingly, this was reflected in the amounts of the more abundant DAG species (Figure 6B and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomic data shown in Figure 6A, E, B, and F.

claim: In the muscle there were no other significant changes in total levels of other lipid species (sphingomyelin [SM], phosphatidylcholine [PC], phosphatidylethanolamine [PE], or phosphatidylserine [PS]).
source: In the muscle there were no other significant changes in total levels of other lipid species (sphingomyelin [SM], phosphatidylcholine [PC], phosphatidylethanolamine [PE], or phosphatidylserine [PS]; Figure 6A), although there were some changes in specific species (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomic data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In the liver there were increases in total levels of PE and cholesterol esters (CE).
source: In the liver there were increases in total levels of PE and cholesterol esters (CE; Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomic data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Almost all the CE species were greater in the dietary intervention groups compared to chow, with six out of the nine species being increased to a greater extent in the Hi-ST group.
source: There was no clear pattern to changes in PE species, but almost all the CE species were greater in the dietary intervention groups compared to chow, with six out of the nine species being increased to a greater extent in the Hi-ST group (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomic data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The increase in CE is not surprising in the Hi-ST animals since the same precursor, acetyl-CoA, is used in both DNL and CE synthesis.
source: This increase in CE is not surprising in the Hi-ST animals since the same precursor, acetyl-CoA, is used in both DNL and CE synthesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on established biochemical knowledge about lipid synthesis pathways.

claim: In quadriceps muscle, Cer18:0 was the predominant lipid species.
source: In quadriceps muscle, Cer18:0 was the predominant lipid species and while it was slightly increased in the Hi-ST animals compared to chow controls, there was a larger increase in the Hi-F group (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomic data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Cer18:0 in muscle was slightly increased in the Hi-ST animals compared to chow controls, with a larger increase in the Hi-F group.
source: In quadriceps muscle, Cer18:0 was the predominant lipid species and while it was slightly increased in the Hi-ST animals compared to chow controls, there was a larger increase in the Hi-F group (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomic data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Cer18:0 in muscle was inversely correlated with glucose uptake measured in the same muscle.
source: The Cer18:0 was also inversely correlated with glucose uptake measured in the same muscle (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: In the liver, Cer22:0, Cer24:0, and Cer24:1 were the predominant ceramide species.
source: In the liver, Cer22:0, Cer24:0, and Cer24:1 were the predominant ceramide species.
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomic data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Cer22:0 was the only abundant ceramide species in liver that significantly changed with diet and demonstrated the same pattern as observed for liver insulin action.
source: Of these abundant species, Cer22:0 was the only one that significantly changed with diet and demonstrated the same pattern as observed for liver insulin action (i.e. suppression of HGO during the clamp).
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomic data and clamp measurements.

claim: Cer22:0 levels in liver were considerably higher in the Hi-F compared to chows with the Hi-ST being intermediate between the two.
source: Specifically, Cer22:0 levels were considerably higher in the Hi-F compared to chows with the Hi-ST being intermediate between the two (Figure 6G).
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomic data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Cer22:0 in liver was negatively correlated with suppression of HGO, an index of liver insulin action.
source: This species of ceramide was negatively correlated with suppression of HGO, an index of liver insulin action (Figure 6H).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Cer20:0 in liver showed a similar pattern of abundance to Cer22:0 and negative correlation with insulin action.
source: Cer20:0, while lower in total levels, showed a similar pattern of abundance (Figure 6G) and negative correlation with insulin action (r2=0.139, p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomic data and correlation analysis.

claim: The relationship between body fat content and insulin action is usually considered to be a negative one, where increasing body fat is associated with a reduction in insulin action.
source: The relationship between body fat content and insulin action is usually considered to be a negative one, where increasing body fat is associated with a reduction in insulin action (Gan et al., 2003; Owei et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about established scientific knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: There have been several reports of individuals with significant obesity but little, or no, difference in metabolic parameters such as insulin resistance when compared to a lean healthy group of individuals.
source: However, there have now been several reports of individuals with significant obesity but little, or no, difference in metabolic parameters such as insulin resistance when compared to a lean healthy group of individuals (Tonks et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tonks et al., 2016.

claim: What makes obese individuals apparently protected from metabolic disease remains unclear.
source: What makes these obese individuals apparently protected from metabolic disease remains unclear and although there are some mouse models that exhibit a similar obese, insulin-sensitive phenotype these have been produced by genetic manipulations (Hotamisligil et al., 1996; Kim et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific knowledge.

claim: Some mouse models exhibit an obese, insulin-sensitive phenotype produced by genetic manipulations.
source: What makes these obese individuals apparently protected from metabolic disease remains unclear and although there are some mouse models that exhibit a similar obese, insulin-sensitive phenotype these have been produced by genetic manipulations (Hotamisligil et al., 1996; Kim et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hotamisligil et al., 1996 and Kim et al., 2007.

claim: Animal models used to investigate the relationship between obesity and insulin action often use a diet high in fat and high in simple carbohydrates (sucrose, fructose) to cause fat gain, insulin resistance, and hepatic steatosis.
source: Animal models used to investigate the relationship between obesity and insulin action often use a diet high in fat and high in simple carbohydrates (sucrose, fructose) to cause fat gain, insulin resistance, and hepatic steatosis (Kim et al., 1999; Malik et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kim et al., 1999 and Malik et al., 2010.

claim: Dietary manipulation models in mice may have more relevance to humans than monogenic models of obesity as overconsumption of calories invariably leads to an increase in fat mass in both mice and humans.
source: Dietary manipulation models in mice may have more relevance to humans than monogenic models of obesity as overconsumption of calories invariably leads to an increase in fat mass in both mice and humans.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the relevance of different animal models.

claim: Adipocytes are unlikely to mediate the maintenance of whole body sensitivity in Hi-ST mice as absolute mass, adipocyte size, and adipose tissue depot insulin sensitivity were similar between Hi-ST and Hi-F fed mice.
source: Our results suggest that adipocytes are unlikely to mediate the maintenance of whole body sensitivity in Hi-ST mice as absolute mass, adipocyte size (i.e. cross-sectional area), and adipose tissue depot insulin sensitivity were similar between Hi-ST and Hi-F fed mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from adipocyte measurements and insulin sensitivity data.

claim: The tissues responsible for the bulk of whole body glucose metabolism, liver and muscle, were more likely to exhibit differences that contribute to understanding of the maintenance of clamp insulin sensitivity in the presence of obesity in Hi-ST fed mice.
source: Therefore, the tissues responsible for the bulk of whole body glucose metabolism, liver and muscle, were more likely to exhibit differences that contribute to our understanding of the maintenance of clamp insulin sensitivity in the presence of obesity in Hi-ST fed mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the role of liver and muscle in glucose metabolism.

claim: There were differences in basal insulinaemia and insulin response during the glucose tolerance test that indicate metabolic differences between chow and Hi-ST mice even though measures of glucose tolerance and clamp insulin sensitivity were similar.
source: However, there were differences in basal insulinaemia and insulin response during the glucose tolerance test that indicate that there were metabolic differences between chow and Hi-ST mice even though measures of glucose tolerance and clamp insulin sensitivity were similar.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from insulin measurements during GTT.

claim: Differences in ectopic triglyceride levels in liver and muscle cannot explain the divergent insulin action in Hi-ST and Hi-F mice.
source: Interestingly, despite the preservation of clamp insulin sensitivity in Hi-ST mice, both liver and muscle of these mice had equivalent amounts of triglyceride storage as observed in Hi-F mice (Figure 4). Therefore, differences in ectopic triglyceride levels in liver and muscle cannot explain the divergent insulin action in Hi-ST and Hi-F mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from triglyceride measurements and insulin sensitivity data.

claim: Upregulation of pathways converting carbohydrate to lipid could underpin the ability of Hi-ST mice to clear glucose and maintain insulin sensitivity.
source: This suggests that upregulation of pathways converting carbohydrate to lipid could underpin the ability of Hi-ST mice to clear glucose and maintain insulin sensitivity.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the DNL and enzyme activity data.

claim: Synthesising fat for storage from dietary carbohydrate is less detrimental to insulin action and glucose homeostasis than metabolising and storing fat from the diet.
source: This data indicates that synthesising fat for storage from dietary carbohydrate is less detrimental to insulin action and glucose homeostasis than metabolising and storing fat from the diet.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing Hi-ST and Hi-F outcomes.

claim: An animal consuming mainly carbohydrate would maintain or increase capacity for utilising this nutrient even if the end result is storage of triglyceride, while an animal consuming mainly fat would increase capacity for utilising fat and downregulate carbohydrate metabolic pathways.
source: It seems mechanistically plausible that an animal consuming mainly carbohydrate would maintain or increase capacity for utilising this nutrient even if the end result is storage of triglyceride, while an animal consuming mainly fat would increase capacity for utilising fat and downregulate carbohydrate metabolic pathways.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation for the observed differences.

claim: Triglycerides are thought to be a metabolically benign form of lipid.
source: Since triglycerides are thought to be a metabolically benign form of lipid, we performed targeted lipidomic analysis on muscle and liver of the clamped mice to investigate changes in other lipid species.
evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Ceramides have been shown previously to correlate with insulin sensitivity/resistance.
source: Differences in lipid species were detected between Hi-F and Hi-ST, particularly in ceramides, that have been shown previously to correlate with insulin sensitivity/resistance (Tonks et al., 2016; Turpin-Nolan et al., 2019; Bergman et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tonks et al., 2016; Turpin-Nolan et al., 2019; Bergman et al., 2016.

claim: In humans, obese, insulin-sensitive individuals have similar levels of Cer18:0 to lean individuals, while obese, insulin-resistant individuals had increased levels.
source: This is similar to the observation in humans where obese, insulin-sensitive individuals have similar levels of Cer18:0 to lean individuals, while obese, insulin-resistant individuals had increased levels (Tonks et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tonks et al., 2016.

claim: Previous studies have shown Cer18:0 content in muscle to be increased in mice fed a Hi-F diet.
source: Previous studies have also shown Cer18:0 content in muscle to be increased in mice fed a Hi-F diet (Turner et al., 2013; Turpin-Nolan et al., 2019; Frangioudakis et al., 2010) while reductions of Cer18:0, through deletion of ceramide synthase 1, has been associated with improved glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity (Turpin-Nolan et al., 2019; Błachnio-Zabielska et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Turner et al., 2013; Turpin-Nolan et al., 2019; Frangioudakis et al., 2010.

claim: Reductions of Cer18:0, through deletion of ceramide synthase 1, has been associated with improved glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity.
source: Previous studies have also shown Cer18:0 content in muscle to be increased in mice fed a Hi-F diet (Turner et al., 2013; Turpin-Nolan et al., 2019; Frangioudakis et al., 2010) while reductions of Cer18:0, through deletion of ceramide synthase 1, has been associated with improved glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity (Turpin-Nolan et al., 2019; Błachnio-Zabielska et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Turpin-Nolan et al., 2019; Błachnio-Zabielska et al., 2022.

claim: A similar relationship between muscle Cer18:0 and insulin sensitivity has previously been demonstrated in humans.
source: A similar relationship has previously been demonstrated in humans (Bergman et al., 2016; Perreault et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bergman et al., 2016; Perreault et al., 2018.

claim: The relationship between muscle Cer18:0 and insulin sensitivity has not always been found.
source: However, this relationship has not always been found (Turner et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Turner et al., 2018.

claim: DAGs are postulated to be mediators of insulin resistance, providing a link between increased lipid and reduced insulin-stimulated glucose uptake.
source: DAGs are postulated to be mediators of insulin resistance, providing a link between increased lipid and reduced insulin-stimulated glucose uptake (Birkenfeld and Shulman, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Birkenfeld and Shulman, 2014.

claim: DAG content was increased in the Hi-F and the Hi-ST muscle to a similar extent and therefore cannot explain the differential insulin action observed between Hi-ST and Hi-F mice.
source: DAG content was increased in the Hi-F and the Hi-ST muscle to a similar extent and therefore cannot explain the differential insulin action observed between Hi-ST and Hi-F mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from DAG measurements and insulin sensitivity data.

claim: Increased Cer18:0 is more closely linked to the development of (Hi-F) skeletal muscle insulin resistance.
source: Taken together, our data suggests that increased Cer18:0 is more closely linked to the development of (Hi-F) skeletal muscle insulin resistance.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from ceramide and insulin sensitivity data.

claim: It has been suggested that changes in ceramide levels reduce insulin action by altering insulin signalling.
source: Mechanistically, it has been suggested that changes in ceramide levels reduce insulin action by altering insulin signalling (Summers et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Summers et al., 2019.

claim: The mechanism relating changes in ceramide to reduced insulin-stimulated glucose uptake in muscle are not well defined and require further investigation.
source: Interestingly, we observed no difference in insulin-stimulated phosphorylation of Akt in all three dietary groups suggesting that the mechanism relating changes in ceramide to reduced insulin-stimulated glucose uptake in muscle are not well defined and require further investigation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of differences in Akt phosphorylation despite differences in insulin sensitivity.

claim: It has been suggested that the cellular distribution of DAGs and ceramides is more relevant to changes in insulin action than the total levels in tissue.
source: Another point to consider is that it has been suggested that the cellular distribution of DAGs, and ceramides, is more relevant to changes in insulin action than the total levels in tissue (Perreault et al., 2018; Szendroedi et al., 2014; Chung et al., 2017), but this was not investigated in our study.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Perreault et al., 2018; Szendroedi et al., 2014; Chung et al., 2017.

claim: The differences in insulin sensitivity observed in liver of Hi-ST and Hi-F mice are unlikely to be directly linked to differences in total DAG levels or differences in specific species.
source: In the liver, DAGs were increased in both the Hi-F and Hi-ST to a similar degree when compared to the chow controls and therefore the differences in insulin sensitivity observed in liver of Hi-ST and Hi-F mice are unlikely to be directly linked to differences in total DAG levels or differences in specific species (although the caveat of DAG cellular distribution still remains).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from DAG measurements and insulin sensitivity data.

claim: Cer22:0 in liver may be involved in the development of insulin resistance.
source: Cer22:0 was also negatively correlated with the suppression of HGO, indicating that it may be involved in the development of insulin resistance.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the correlation data.

claim: Previous studies have shown Cer22:0 to be increased in livers of people with type 2 diabetes.
source: Previous studies have shown Cer22:0 to be increased in livers of people with type 2 diabetes (Razak Hady et al., 2019) and Hi-F fed rodents (Turner et al., 2013; Montgomery et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Razak Hady et al., 2019; Turner et al., 2013; Montgomery et al., 2016.

claim: Some studies investigating the role of ceramides in liver insulin resistance have implicated Cer16:0 as an important species.
source: Some studies investigating the role of ceramides in liver insulin resistance have implicated Cer16:0 as an important species (Raichur et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Raichur et al., 2019.

claim: Cer16:0 in liver was higher in the Hi-F animals but did not reach statistical significance.
source: In our study, this species was higher in the Hi-F animals but did not reach statistical significance.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of lipidomic data.

claim: Hi-F diet-induced insulin resistance in muscle and liver is associated with increased DAG and ceramide levels.
source: Our study clearly indicates that Hi-F diet-induced insulin resistance in muscle and liver is associated with increased DAG and ceramide levels, but that only lower levels of specific ceramides species correlate with the maintenance of insulin sensitivity, despite significant obesity and accumulation of tissue TAG in Hi-ST mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined lipidomic and insulin sensitivity data.

claim: Only lower levels of specific ceramides species correlate with the maintenance of insulin sensitivity, despite significant obesity and accumulation of tissue TAG in Hi-ST mice.
source: Our study clearly indicates that Hi-F diet-induced insulin resistance in muscle and liver is associated with increased DAG and ceramide levels, but that only lower levels of specific ceramides species correlate with the maintenance of insulin sensitivity, despite significant obesity and accumulation of tissue TAG in Hi-ST mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined lipidomic and insulin sensitivity data.

claim: While the majority of obese people exhibit some level of insulin resistance, there are obese individuals of both genders who have metabolic profiles indistinguishable from lean individuals.
source: While the majority of obese people exhibit some level of insulin resistance, there are obese individuals of both genders who have metabolic profiles indistinguishable from lean individuals (Smith et al., 2019; Samocha-Bonet et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Smith et al., 2019; Samocha-Bonet et al., 2012.

claim: Whether obese, insulin-sensitive people are on a trajectory to inevitable metabolic disease or have a genetic background or lifestyle that protects against metabolic disease, despite obesity, remains an area of current research interest.
source: Whether these obese, insulin-sensitive people are on a trajectory to inevitable metabolic disease or have a genetic background or lifestyle that protects against metabolic disease, despite obesity, remains an area of current research interest.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific knowledge and ongoing research questions.

claim: One recent systematic review suggests that healthy eating patterns can influence the metabolic profile of otherwise obese individuals.
source: One recent systematic review (Vilela et al., 2021) suggests that healthy eating patterns can influence the metabolic profile of otherwise obese individuals while other reviews suggest the variation in criteria used to classify obese metabolically healthy people make it difficult to draw conclusions about mechanisms for metabolic differences in similarly obese individuals (Gómez-Zorita et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Vilela et al., 2021.

claim: Other reviews suggest the variation in criteria used to classify obese metabolically healthy people make it difficult to draw conclusions about mechanisms for metabolic differences in similarly obese individuals.
source: One recent systematic review (Vilela et al., 2021) suggests that healthy eating patterns can influence the metabolic profile of otherwise obese individuals while other reviews suggest the variation in criteria used to classify obese metabolically healthy people make it difficult to draw conclusions about mechanisms for metabolic differences in similarly obese individuals (Gómez-Zorita et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gómez-Zorita et al., 2021.

claim: It remains a possibility that the current diet may have a significant impact on insulin sensitivity irrespective of the obesity status of an individual.
source: As reflected in our results in mice, it remains a possibility that the current diet may have a significant impact on insulin sensitivity irrespective of the obesity status of an individual.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the study results.

claim: The availability of specific types of nutrients can alter glucose homeostasis in animals and humans.
source: It is well documented that the availability of specific types of nutrients can alter glucose homeostasis in animals and humans.
evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Acute infusion of lipids lowers insulin sensitivity within a few hours in humans and animals.
source: Acute infusion of lipids lowers insulin sensitivity within a few hours in humans and animals (Dubé et al., 2014; Hoy et al., 2009) and people undergoing routine screening with an oGTT are advised to consume largely carbohydrate foods for 24–48 hr before testing because of the effects of consuming fatty foods on subsequent glucose clearance (Kaneko et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dubé et al., 2014; Hoy et al., 2009.

claim: People undergoing routine screening with an oGTT are advised to consume largely carbohydrate foods for 24–48 hr before testing because of the effects of consuming fatty foods on subsequent glucose clearance.
source: Acute infusion of lipids lowers insulin sensitivity within a few hours in humans and animals (Dubé et al., 2014; Hoy et al., 2009) and people undergoing routine screening with an oGTT are advised to consume largely carbohydrate foods for 24–48 hr before testing because of the effects of consuming fatty foods on subsequent glucose clearance (Kaneko et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kaneko et al., 1998.

claim: A proportion of insulin action is adaptive and may be modulated by changing the diet over a relatively short period.
source: Together, this data suggests that a proportion of insulin action is adaptive and may be modulated by changing the diet over a relatively short period.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the cited evidence about acute dietary effects.

claim: This adaptive mechanism would enable organisms to conserve glucose for tissues unable to utilise fatty acids, such as the brain and central nervous system, during periods of carbohydrate scarcity.
source: This mechanism would enable organisms to conserve glucose for tissues unable to utilise fatty acids, such as the brain and central nervous system, during periods of carbohydrate scarcity.
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary/physiological explanation for the adaptive insulin action.

claim: Mice fed a Hi-ST diet remain glucose tolerant and insulin sensitive despite having excess adipose tissue.
source: Overall, our findings that mice fed a Hi-ST diet remain glucose tolerant and insulin sensitive despite having excess adipose tissue demonstrates that recent nutritional intake is an important factor in determining glucose homeostasis.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental findings.

claim: Recent nutritional intake is an important factor in determining glucose homeostasis.
source: Overall, our findings that mice fed a Hi-ST diet remain glucose tolerant and insulin sensitive despite having excess adipose tissue demonstrates that recent nutritional intake is an important factor in determining glucose homeostasis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The Hi-ST fed mice were not identical to lean control mice (they exhibited basal hyperglycaemia and hyperinsulinaemia).
source: Although the Hi-ST fed mice were not identical to lean control mice (they exhibited basal hyperglycaemia and hyperinsulinaemia), this dietary rodent model of insulin-sensitive obesity may be useful for investigating mechanisms involved in obesity-related insulin resistance.
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements of basal glucose and insulin levels.

claim: This dietary rodent model of insulin-sensitive obesity may be useful for investigating mechanisms involved in obesity-related insulin resistance.
source: Although the Hi-ST fed mice were not identical to lean control mice (they exhibited basal hyperglycaemia and hyperinsulinaemia), this dietary rodent model of insulin-sensitive obesity may be useful for investigating mechanisms involved in obesity-related insulin resistance.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential utility of the model.

claim: The differences in lipid composition in skeletal muscle and liver between Hi-ST and Hi-F mice support the idea that individual lipid species may be more important determinants of insulin resistance than total lipid levels.
source: The differences in lipid composition in skeletal muscle and liver between Hi-ST and Hi-F mice also support the idea that individual lipid species may be more important determinants of insulin resistance than total lipid levels and therapeutic approaches that alter these specific lipids could have beneficial metabolic effects.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lipidomic data.

claim: Therapeutic approaches that alter specific lipid species could have beneficial metabolic effects.
source: The differences in lipid composition in skeletal muscle and liver between Hi-ST and Hi-F mice also support the idea that individual lipid species may be more important determinants of insulin resistance than total lipid levels and therapeutic approaches that alter these specific lipids could have beneficial metabolic effects.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic implications.
